title: Pipa the king
hookLine: a king turned devotee sings that the body itself is the temple (Dhanasri, Pipa, ang 695)

lines: A KING WHO LEFT THE THRONE.
cards: A king has everything a temple needs: money for the marble, priests on the payroll, gold for the lamps. Tradition says Pipa was a king like that, who left his throne to follow the path of devotion.
So when he sings about where God is worshipped, you might expect a grand building. Instead, on the same page as Dhanna and Sain, Pipa points somewhere much closer. It's been with you all day.

teach.b: Pipa's hymn is in Raag Dhanasri, on Ang 695, and its key word is kaaiaa, the body.

teach.h: DEITY, TEMPLE, PILGRIM, LAMP: ALL WITHIN.
teach.b: In paraphrase, it opens: the body is the deity, the body is the temple, the body is the pilgrim. Within the body are the incense, the lamp and the offerings of food, and the leaves laid down in worship.

Hear it next to yesterday. Sain set out incense, lamp and ghee on the tray, then offered himself. Pipa takes the whole tray and moves it inside: temple, pilgrim, lamp and offering, all found in the body.
Then a search. In paraphrase: I searched through many realms, and found the treasures within the body. Nothing comes and nothing goes.

teach.h: WHAT'S IN THE UNIVERSE IS IN THE BODY.
teach.b: And a line worth holding onto: what is in the universe is in the body; whoever searches, finds. The hymn closes: Pipa prays, the supreme essence is there, and the True Guru reveals it. Two things to notice.
This isn't about the body as something to perfect or show off. It's the place where the sacred is met, the ordinary one, tired or sick or young or old.
And it isn't a do-it-yourself map: Pipa ends with the True Guru, the one who shows you what was there all along. A king who could have paid for any temple, saying: the temple was here.

how: Pipa's hymn is sung in gurdwaras as part of the Guru Granth Sahib, on the same page as the hymns of Dhanna and Sain.

o: the body, where Pipa finds the temple
the soul that leaves the body at death
a temple built of marble and gold

s: Pipa's hymn is about building a grand temple
it says the body itself is the deity, the temple and the pilgrim.
Pipa says anyone can find it alone, no guide needed
the hymn closes: the True Guru reveals the supreme essence.
Pipa's hymn is on the same page as Sain's and Dhanna's
all three are in Raag Dhanasri on Ang 695.

games.q: you're Pipa, and you've searched through many realms looking for the treasure. where do you find it?
o: in the royal treasury you left.
games.why: within the body, he sings: what is in the universe is in the body, and whoever searches, finds.

practice: Walk through your body gently, the way a pilgrim walks into a holy place: the feet that carried you here, the hands that worked, the chest rising and falling. Whatever aches, let it be part of the temple too, without judging it.
If you pray, say Waheguru as you breathe out.

wordCard.voice: Kaaiaa. Pipa's word for the body: the deity, the temple and the pilgrim all found within it, with the True Guru showing what's there.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: the body, the word Pipa's hymn turns into a temple (Ang 695).

carryVoice: Your line: the body is the temple. The week went from dead cattle to a farmer's list, a barber's lamp and a king's temple. Day seven hundred eighty-four, done.

sources.ref: Dhanasri, Pipa (kaayau devaa kaaiau deval), Ang 695
